A Python Enhancement Proposal lists this idea as rejected:
Title: We have decided to disallow (for the time being) using escaped braces (\{ and \}) in addition to…
Text: We have decided to disallow (for the time being) using escaped braces (\{ and \}) in addition to the {{ and }} syntax. Although the authors of the PEP believe that allowing escaped braces is a good idea, we have decided to not include it in this PEP, as it is not strictly necessary for the formalization of f-strings proposed here, and it can be added independently in a regular CPython issue.

Ideas found by reading the public discussion:
0. Restrict or allow arbitrary nesting of quotes/braces in f-strings [rejected] - The idea of limiting quote reuse or nesting was rejected because it would significantly increase parser maintenance costs. Reasons: Another option here is to restrict arbitrary nesting to a specific depth. I think that will allow regex-based lexers to work at the price of having some complex regular expression.; Ignoring the consistency arguments, limiting quote reuse raises quite a lot the complexity. This is because when parsing the expression part now the parser needs to be aware that is parsing an expression inside an f-string with a given quite...; I am not sure what we finally propose (quote reuse or not) as we want to gather some feedback first, but we will discuss this aspect among authors again.; Nested f-strings like f"{f"infinite"}" are incredibly difficult for a human to parse IMHO and require tools to be aligned about how to help the user understand them.; By keeping the quote restriction, arbitrary nesting can be prevented while still simplifying implementation and removing annoying bits like backslash limitations.; Preventing nesting entirely wouldn't be backwards compatible, f-strings can already be nested if you use different quote styles for each level.; I believe that when PEP 498 was discussed, there was a good reason to use the latter, but somehow I can't find that reason in the PEP; In any case, I think the question is if we can support both, right (for backwards compat). The double { makes it somehow harder to implement; The doubling has always irked me, and I think I've forgotten that it existed several times over the years; In any case, I think the question is if we can support both, right (for backwards compat). The double { makes it somehow harder to implement but I don't think there is a way around supporting it
1. Document IDLE limitations and PEP 8 guidance regarding quote reuse in f-strings [accepted] - The PEP was updated to document that IDLE cannot properly handle f-strings reusing opening quotes and users should avoid reformatters. Reasons: If quote reuse stays, please do so. The SC should know that approving this as is will break a few things. Perhaps add at least “Lexing all possible f-strings with relational expressions will no longer be possible. In particular, reuse of opening quotes in replacement fields will be a problem.”; I would also like to see the PEP more strongly discourage actually relying on that in manually written code, in the form of a proposed addition to PEP 8.; The section on string quotes would be the appropriate place for an addition like: (The part in parentheses probably shouldn't be added to PEP 8)
2. Tokenization details, token names, and preventing f-strings from looking like regular strings [rejected] - The idea that f-strings should strictly look like regular strings without allowing non-intuitive quoting was rejected in favor of flexibility. Reasons: IMO f-strings should continue to look like regular Python strings to a Python programmer and not allow non-intuitive quoting just because the parser can handle this...; I don't think that nesting f-strings should be allowed, but I guess that ship has already sailed.; The tokens in the PEP are there just for reference to understand what they do but they are an implementation detail and not a public API definition.; The tokenizer module in the reference implementation seems to have not caught up with the PEP yet because it is Python and not the private C implementation.; What these tokens (the ones in the C tokenizer, which I insist is not visible) will contain is going to be based fundamentally on what makes the implementation simpler.; In general, you should not focus on what the tokens contain.; I apologize if it seems that I am overly insisting on this, but I think is important because the proposal doesn't change any user-visible thing if the tokens contain the starting quote or not; I think it would help if there was a specification for the tokens – not for what is returned by the tokenizer, but e.g. a regular expression showing what the lexer accepts for each token.; I don't think a regular expression is possible (or at least straightforward so it helps for clarifications) because the cut points depend on the level of parenthesis

best: the number of the idea that is the SAME idea as the rejected one, or -1 if none of them is.
reasons_agree: if there is a match, do its reasons agree with the reason the proposal gives?
"yes" (same reason), "partial" (overlapping), "no" (different). If best is -1, answer "no".
